The Yellowmouth barracuda Sphyraena viridensis is a predatory teleost inhabiting the subtropical waters of the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Upon hatching, the prolarva emerges from its transparent, pelagic egg at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0016 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0016 grams]. This yolk-dependent, lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its endogenous reserves during the first days post-eclosion, and the transition to active feeding occurs shortly after the yolk-sac is fully resorbed. Survey data from the waters around the Azores have documented the species' ultimate fork length at 125 centimeters [Li = 125 centimeters], making it one of the larger members of its genus. This asymptotic size places S. viridensis among the apex predators of its pelagic-reef interface habitat, capable of preying on a wide range of smaller fish and cephalopods. Growth trajectories derived from length-frequency distributions suggest that individuals approach this maximum size only after several years of sustained feeding, a pattern consistent with the energetic demands of maintaining such a large body in a resource-limited environment. The species' rapid burst speed and streamlined morphology are well adapted for ambush predation in clear, sunlit waters.

Puberty in Sphyraena viridensis occurs at a fork length of approximately 53 centimeters [Lp = approximately 53 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 785 grams [Wwp = 785 grams]. This size at maturity is consistent with the general pattern observed among congeneric barracudas, in which reproductive capability is delayed until a substantial portion of the ultimate body size has been attained. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected in the Mediterranean indicates that vitellogenesis onset and spermiation onset occur synchronously with the attainment of this length, suggesting a tight coupling between somatic growth and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. The progressive gonad maturation that follows is accompanied by observable changes in the coloration of the caudal fin and the characteristic yellow hue of the mouth that gives the species its common name. Individuals that have not yet reached this length are classified as immature post-metamorphic juveniles and do not participate in the annual spawning aggregations that form over rocky substrates during the summer months. The reproductive activation is likely modulated by the seasonal warming of surface waters, which serves as an environmental cue for the initiation of gametogenesis.

The maximum reproductive rate of Sphyraena viridensis has been studied under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C], yielding valuable insights into the species' potential fecundity. Gravid females maintained at this thermal regime produce approximately 2466 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2466 eggs per day], reflecting a remarkably high daily reproductive output characteristic of many tropical and subtropical scombrid and sphyraenid species that inhabit warm, productive waters. The eggs themselves are small, buoyant, and pelagic, dispersing widely with ocean currents before hatching. This high-frequency, low-investment per egg reproductive strategy is energetically demanding, requiring females to maintain a steady intake of lipid-rich prey throughout the protracted spawning window. The temperature dependence of this rate is noteworthy, as deviations from 18.3 °C can significantly alter the interval between successive spawning events.

The ultimate wet weight reported for Sphyraena viridensis, derived from the species' asymptotic length, reaches 9,600 grams [Wwi = 9,600 grams]. This substantial body mass, attained by the oldest and largest individuals, underscores the species' position as a significant biomass contributor within its coastal and pelagic ecosystems. Comparatively, the body mass at which sexual maturation occurs reaches 785 grams [Wwp = 785 grams], representing only about 8 percent of this ultimate mass, indicating that individuals begin their reproductive careers while still undergoing considerable somatic growth. This pattern of early maturation relative to final size is common among fast-growing, iteroparous marine predators. The period following puberty is characterized by a gradual deceleration of growth, with available data from otolith-based age and growth studies showing that females tend to reach larger asymptotic weights than males, a common phenomenon in barracudas likely linked to the energetic overhead of egg production. The conversion of length to mass follows a power-law relationship typical of fusiform teleosts, and the species' condition factor varies seasonally in response to prey availability and reproductive state. Specimens exceeding 8,000 grams are considered trophy catches and are relatively rare in sampled populations.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Sphyraena viridensis, based on otolith annulus counts from individuals captured in the wild, is 12 years [am = 12 years] when maintained under the thermal conditions typical of its subtropical range, approximately 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C]. This longevity is moderate among large-bodied sphyraenids, with some congeneric species reported to live considerably longer in cooler waters where metabolic rates are lower. The age structure of populations sampled in the Mediterranean suggests that natural mortality is relatively low among post-pubertal adults, but that senescence may set in after roughly a decade, leading to a decline in condition and increased susceptibility to predation. Very old individuals, those exceeding 10 years, are rarely encountered in fisheries landings, which may reflect either their low abundance or their ability to avoid capture through learned behavior. The species is estimated to survive up to 12 years [am = up to 12 years] under natural conditions; in warmer peripheral portions of the species' range, life expectancy may be somewhat reduced due to the accelerated metabolic costs associated with elevated temper at a temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C]atures. Comparative studies of growth increments in S. viridensis suggest that sexual dimorphism in longevity is minimal, with both sexes displaying similar maximum ages. The species' relatively late age at maturity, combined with its moderate lifespan, places it on the slower end of the fast-slow life-history continuum for pelagic piscivores, a strategy that buffers against the stochasticity of prey availability in its dynamic coastal environment.
